claims.text: Conventional powder-metallurgy or sintering routes for W particles or connected W regions in a Cu matrix typically leave residual voids and phase mismatch.
An ultrathin nickel coating can be deposited electrolessly on tungsten particles before incorporation into a copper matrix.
The deposited nickel layer will form an interfacial bridge between tungsten and copper.
A nickel interlayer will improve bonding between tungsten and copper.
Nickel acts as a wetting promoter at a W–Cu interface.
Nickel acts as a diffusion barrier at a W–Cu interface.
The nickel layer reduces surface-energy differences between tungsten and copper.
Nickel-enhanced wetting minimizes void formation during sintering.
Nickel-enhanced wetting minimizes W–Cu phase separation during sintering.
The nickel interlayer preserves mechanical continuity under cyclic high-heat and irradiation loading.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have higher thermal conductivity than otherwise identically processed composites containing uncoated tungsten.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have fewer interfacial defects than composites containing uncoated tungsten.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will maintain or improve mechanical durability relative to composites containing uncoated tungsten.
Fusion divertor materials experience high thermal flux and irradiation involving energetic electrons and ions.
Existing relevant studies include 6 MeV electron irradiation and Ar+, He+, and D+ ion irradiation tests.
Approximately 1100 °C is a relevant upper processing or annealing boundary for the proposed W–Cu/Ni composite.
A thermal interlayer is needed between tungsten plasma-facing material and CuCrZr cooling structures because their working-temperature ranges differ.
Spark-plasma-sintered or vapor-coated-W baselines typically have microstructural defects and imperfect W–Cu contact.
The optimal nickel-layer thickness and its long-term irradiation stability are undetermined.
Scale-up and processing impurities may affect the composite's performance.

contradictions.description: The intervention defines particle pre-coating as an interfacial modification, while the baseline groups vapor-coated W powders under methods described as being 'without interfacial modification.' Vapor coating is itself an interfacial modification, so the baseline category is internally inconsistent.
The conditions allow temperatures up to approximately 1100 °C, whereas the boundary states a strict limit below 1100 °C. This is a minor ambiguity in whether operation at 1100 °C is included.
